name: Kulsab
confidence_why: Word-final stress for Kursav (Kulsab) is inferred from Daniels (2010: 168), who after fieldwork across the Sogeram family wrote that stress is 'almost always word-final in the daughter languages' and reconstructed final stress for Proto-Sogeram; no work describes Kursav stress directly (Daniels' 2015 Kursav grammar sketch and his 2020 monograph are silent on it and call Sogeram stress systems a matter for further research), and nothing contradicts final stress.
catalog_citation: Daniels, Don R. 2010. A preliminary phonological history of the Sogeram languages of Papua New Guinea. Oceanic Linguistics 49(1): 163-193. doi:10.1353/ol.0.0068
catalog_locator: Sec. 2 'Proto-Sogeram', p. 168 (p. 7 of the 32-page Project MUSE copy), the sentence immediately after the PSOG inventory (1); echoed sec. 4.1.2 p. 175. Kulsab named as one of the eight daughter languages on p. 164 ('Aisi (Musak); Kulsab (Faita)') and in figures 2-3. Sec. 5.3 'Kulsab innovations' pp. 182-183 contains no stress statement.
catalog_quote: Stress is almost always word-final in the daughter languages, and it was probably also word-final in PSOG. The central vowel /ɨ/ behaves as a neutral vowel in the family, arising paragogically and epenthetically in many situations (cf. 3.1.2, 3.1.4, and 4.4.1), and being the result of any vowel-centering processes (such as 4.1.2. and 5.2.4). [p. 168] ... Unrounded vowels in closed penults centered to /ɨ/ when followed by open ultimas; the fact that PSOG probably had word-final stress helps motivate this change. [p. 175]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for fait1240; this is the first statement bearing on Kulsab stress, but it is a generalisation over all Sogeram daughter languages, not a Kulsab-specific description. Daniels 2020 (p. 84) says the 2010 Kulsab inventory 'was based on poorer data and was inaccurate in several respects', which lowers the weight of any Kulsab inference from this paper.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level generalisation only: in the Sogeram daughter languages (of which Kulsab is one) word stress is 'almost always' on the final syllable, and Proto-Sogeram is reconstructed with final stress. The paper never states where stress falls in Kulsab itself; its Kulsab section (pp. 182-183) covers the segmental inventory (12), ɨ-loss, i-lowering and genitive prefixes, and notes the data came from two elderly semi-speakers with heavy Mesop/Gende borrowing.
new_statements.exceptions: 'almost always' hedges the family-level claim; no language-specific exceptions named; no Kulsab examples with stress marked.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works treat the same language under different names: 'Kulsab' in Daniels 2010, 'Kursav' in Daniels 2020 (village name Faita; Z'graggen's 'Faita', Brahman group). Daniels 2010 p. 183 suggests Z'graggen's 1980 wordlist came from another Kulsab dialect that had borrowed Mesop vocabulary; Daniels' own data are from two elderly semi-speakers (2010) and 2014 fieldwork (2020).

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources. Daniels 2010 (p. 168) states stress is almost always word-final across the Sogeram daughter languages and reconstructs final stress for Proto-Sogeram; Daniels 2020 says nothing about Kursav stress, repeats word-final stress for Manat (p. 65) and calls the stress systems of the Sogeram languages a topic for further research (p. 60). The prior check of Daniels 2015 (Kursav sketch, pp. 883-986) likewise found no Kursav stress statement. The only tension is one of weight: the fixed: final syllable reading for Kulsab rests solely on a hedged family-level generalisation whose Kulsab underpinnings Daniels himself later called poor data.

sources.citation: Daniels, Don Roger. 2015. A Reconstruction of Proto-Sogeram: Phonology, Lexicon, and Morphosyntax. PhD dissertation, University of California, Santa Barbara. 1127 pp. Appendix 5 'Kursav Grammar Sketch' pp. 883-986 (= Glottolog ref 469266); phonology sec. 5.2 pp. 887-892 (PDF 912-917); sec. 2.4.5 'Kursav Innovations' pp. 110-112.https://escholarship.org/content/qt1kj4174g/qt1kj4174g.pdf
sources.note: Nothing for Kursav. Sec. 5.2 (read in full) covers consonant/vowel inventories, allophony, onset clusters with epenthetic [ɨ], diphthongs, word-final high-vowel devoicing/metathesis, /ɨ/ status, vowel elision; no stress/accent/tone statement anywhere in pp. 908-1011 or sec. 2.4.5. Only stress remark in the whole work is p. 71 (Mand): 'Further research into the stress systems of the Sogeram languages might reveal a consistent pattern.'
